title: Lesson 1: Your money
text: > The 30-second version Spend less than you earn, automatically: save on payday, before you can spend it. Keep 3–6 months of essential costs as an emergency fund. Pay off expensive debt first. Compound interest works for you in savings and against you in debt.

title: Lesson 1: Your money: Know where it goes
text: You can't fix what you don't measure. Track every expense for one month before writing any budget — most people underestimate their spending by a wide margin, especially on food and subscriptions. A common starting split is 50/30/20: 50% needs, 30% wants, 20% saving and debt payoff. Treat it as a rough check, not a rule. In expensive cities, needs alone can be 60–70% of take-home pay; that's a signal to work on income or housing cost, not a personal failure. The one habit that matters most Pay yourself first. Set savings to move automatically on payday, so you're budgeting what's left instead of saving what's left.

title: Lesson 1: Your money: Emergency fund
text: Keep 3–6 months of essential expenses in an easy-to-reach, insured savings account. Aim for the higher end if your income is irregular or you support others. This money isn't an investment; its job is to stop a car repair from becoming credit-card debt.

title: Lesson 1: Your money: Debt: good, bad and expensive
text: Debt is a tool. The question is always: does what I'm buying earn or save more than the interest costs? Expensive debt (credit cards, payday loans, often 20–30%+ APR): pay it off before investing. Paying off a 24% card is a guaranteed 24% return — no investment reliably beats that. Moderate debt (car loans, personal loans): keep terms short and avoid borrowing for things that lose value fast. Low-rate debt (some mortgages and student loans): often fine to pay on schedule while you invest. Two payoff methods Method How Honest verdict Avalanche Pay minimums on everything; extra money goes to the highest interest rate. Mathematically cheapest. Always. Snowball Extra money goes to the smallest balance first. Costs more interest, but quick wins keep some people going. The best plan is the one you'll stick to.

title: Lesson 1: Your money: Compound interest
text: Compounding means you earn returns on your earlier returns. Growth starts slow, then accelerates. Future value = Starting amount × (1 + rate)^years Example: $10,000 at 7% for 30 years = 10,000 × 1.07^30 ≈ $76,123 Rule of 72: divide 72 by the yearly rate to estimate how many years it takes money to double. At 8%, about 9 years. At 24% credit-card interest, a balance you ignore doubles in about 3 years.

title: Lesson 1: Your money: Inflation
text: Inflation is prices rising over time, so each dollar buys less. At 3% inflation, $100 today buys only about $74 of today's goods in 10 years. Cash sitting in a 0% account is quietly losing value. That's the reason to invest long-term money, not keep it all in cash.

title: Lesson 1: Your money: Credit scores (US)
text: Lenders use your score to price loans. The rough order of importance: Payment history — never miss a payment. Turn on autopay for at least the minimum. Utilisation — how much of your limit you use. Under 30% is the common guideline; under 10% is better. Length of history — keep old no-fee cards open. Credit mix and new applications — minor factors. Other countries use different scoring systems, though paying on time and using little of your limit help almost everywhere. ← All courses2. Investing →

title: Lesson 2: Investing
text: > The 30-second version Higher returns come with bigger swings. "Guaranteed high returns" is a red flag. Cheap index funds beat most professionals once fees are counted. Fees compound too: 1% a year can cost a fortune over decades.

title: Lesson 2: Investing: Risk and return are linked
text: Higher expected return comes with bigger swings in value. There's no free lunch. Anyone offering high returns with "no risk" is mistaken or lying. Asset What it is Typical role Cash / savings Bank deposits, money-market funds Safety and short-term needs. Loses to inflation over long periods. Bonds Loans to governments or companies that pay interest Steadier than stocks, lower long-run return. Stocks Part-ownership of companies Long-term growth. Can fall 30–50% in a bad year. Real estate Property, or funds that own property Income plus growth. Illiquid and concentrated if you own one house. Time horizon rule of thumb: money you need within about 5 years shouldn't be heavily in stocks. A crash right before you need it can force you to sell at the bottom.

title: Lesson 2: Investing: Diversification and index funds
text: Diversification means not betting everything on one company, sector or country. An index fund buys every company in a market index, such as the S&P 500, for a very low fee. The uncomfortable fact Over 15+ years, the large majority of professional fund managers fail to beat a simple low-cost index fund after fees. If professionals with research teams mostly can't do it, a beginner day-trading on a phone app almost certainly won't.

title: Lesson 2: Investing: Fees matter more than you think
text: A 1% yearly fee sounds tiny. It's charged every year on your whole balance, forever. Made-up example: $100,000 for 30 years at 7% (≈0.05% index fund) → about $761,000 at 6% (same, minus 1% fee) → about $574,000 The 1% fee cost ≈ $187,000

title: Lesson 2: Investing: Retirement accounts (US examples)
text: 401(k) employer match: some employers add money when you save for retirement. The rules vary by employer and plan: how much they match, up to what limit, and how long you must stay before the money is fully yours (called vesting). If your plan has a match, contributing at least enough to get all of it is usually the first step, because a 50% or 100% match is an instant 50–100% return on that money. Check your own plan's rules. Traditional vs Roth: Traditional gives a tax break now and you pay tax later; Roth is taxed now and grows tax-free. Roth tends to suit people who expect a higher tax rate later. Other countries have their own versions (UK ISA/SIPP, Canada TFSA/RRSP, Australia super). The logic is similar: use tax-advantaged accounts first.

title: Lesson 2: Investing: A sensible order of operations
text: Small starter emergency fund. Get any employer match your plan offers. Pay off high-interest debt. Full emergency fund (3–6 months). Max tax-advantaged accounts with low-cost diversified funds. Then taxable investing, extra mortgage payments, and other goals.

title: Lesson 2: Investing: Red flags
text: "Guaranteed" high returns. Pressure to decide today. Returns that are suspiciously smooth. You can't explain how the money is made. Income depends on recruiting others. Influencers paid to promote coins or courses. ← 1. Your money3. Funding & valuation →

title: Lesson 4: How a business makes money
text: > The 30-second version Margin = profit ÷ price. Markup = profit ÷ cost. They are not the same. Break-even = fixed costs ÷ what each sale contributes. Profit is not cash. Watch the bank balance.

title: Lesson 4: How a business makes money: The profit ladder
text: Revenue (what customers paid) − Cost of goods sold (COGS) (direct cost of what you sold) = Gross profit − Operating expenses (rent, salaries, marketing, software) = Operating profit − Interest and taxes = Net profit

title: Lesson 4: How a business makes money: Margin vs markup (people mix these up constantly)
text: Say a product costs you $60 and you sell it for $100. Markup = profit ÷ cost = 40 ÷ 60 = 66.7% Margin = profit ÷ price = 40 ÷ 100 = 40% Same deal, very different numbers. Always ask which one someone means. Margin can never exceed 100%; markup can.

title: Lesson 4: How a business makes money: Fixed costs, variable costs and break-even
text: Fixed costs stay the same however much you sell (rent, base salaries, software). Variable costs rise with each unit (materials, shipping, payment fees). Contribution margin = price − variable cost per unit. It's what each sale contributes towards fixed costs. Break-even units = Fixed costs ÷ (Price − Variable cost per unit) Example: $5,000/month fixed, $25 price, $15 variable = 5,000 ÷ 10 = 500 units a month just to break even

title: Lesson 4: How a business makes money: Unit economics
text: Does each customer make you money? Two numbers answer that: CAC (customer acquisition cost): total sales and marketing spend ÷ new customers. LTV (lifetime value): average revenue per month × gross margin × months a customer stays. A common guideline is LTV at least 3× CAC, and earning back CAC within about 12 months. If LTV is below CAC, growing faster just loses money faster.

title: Lesson 4: How a business makes money: Cash flow is not profit
text: Profit is an accounting idea; cash is what pays the bills. You can be profitable on paper and still go bust if: Customers pay in 60 days but suppliers want payment in 30. Stock (inventory) sits on shelves tying up cash. Fast growth forces you to buy materials before customers pay. The classic killer Lack of cash, not lack of profit, is behind a large share of small-business failures. Watch your bank balance weekly and forecast it 13 weeks ahead.

title: Lesson 4: How a business makes money: Pricing
text: Cost-plus: cost + a markup. Simple, but ignores what customers would pay. Value-based: price based on the value to the customer. Harder, usually more profitable. Why price is powerful: on a 20% margin, a 5% price increase (if volume holds) raises profit by 25%. Most small businesses underprice. ← 3. Funding & valuation5. Financial statements →

title: Lesson 5: Financial statements
text: > The 30-second version Income statement: did we make money? Balance sheet: what we own and owe. Assets = liabilities + equity. Cash flow statement: where the cash actually went.

title: Lesson 5: Financial statements: Income statement — "Did we make money this period?"
text: Revenue, minus costs, equals profit, over a period such as a quarter or year. It's the profit ladder from Lesson 3.

title: Lesson 5: Financial statements: Balance sheet — "What do we own and owe right now?"
text: Assets = Liabilities + Equity Assets: cash, money owed by customers (receivables), inventory, equipment. Liabilities: money owed to others, such as loans, supplier bills (payables) and taxes due. Equity: what's left for the owners. It always balances, because everything the company owns was paid for either with borrowed money or with owners' money.

title: Lesson 5: Financial statements: Cash flow statement — "Where did the cash actually go?"
text: Operating: cash from running the business. This is the most important one. Investing: buying or selling equipment, property or other businesses. Financing: borrowing, repaying loans, raising equity, paying dividends. A healthy mature business usually generates positive operating cash flow. Positive profit with negative operating cash flow year after year is a warning sign.

title: Lesson 5: Financial statements: Ratios worth knowing
text: Ratio Formula Tells you Gross margin Gross profit ÷ Revenue How much each sale leaves after direct costs Net margin Net profit ÷ Revenue What's left after everything Current ratio Current assets ÷ Current liabilities Can it pay bills due in the next year? Below 1 is a caution sign. Debt-to-equity Total liabilities ÷ Equity How much the business relies on borrowing Return on equity (ROE) Net profit ÷ Equity How well it uses owners' money Context beats rules "Good" ratios vary a lot by industry. A supermarket with a 2–3% net margin can be excellent; a software company at 3% might be struggling. Compare a business against its own history and against similar companies, not against a universal number. ← 4. How a business makes money6. Why businesses exist →

title: Lesson 3: Funding & valuation
text: > The 30-second version You can fund a business from savings, a loan, or by selling shares. Each costs you something different. An investor's share = their money ÷ the value after they invest. Money tomorrow is worth less than money today.

title: Lesson 3: Funding & valuation: Three ways to fund a business
text: Source You give up Good when Bootstrapping (own savings, revenue) Speed You can grow from customer money. You keep full control. Debt (loans, credit lines) Fixed repayments plus interest; often a personal guarantee Cash flow is predictable enough to cover repayments. Equity (angels, venture capital) Ownership and some control The business can grow very large, very fast, and needs money to do it. Reality check Most businesses never raise venture capital and shouldn't try. VCs need a few investments to return their whole fund, so they push for huge, risky growth. That's often bad for a business that could be a very good, profitable, smaller company.

title: Lesson 3: Funding & valuation: Dilution
text: Pre-money valuation = value before new money comes in Post-money valuation = pre-money + investment Investor's share = investment ÷ post-money Example: raise $250,000 at $1,000,000 pre-money Post-money = $1,250,000 → investor owns 250k ÷ 1.25M = 20% A smaller slice of a bigger pie can be worth more, but only if the money actually makes the pie bigger.

title: Lesson 3: Funding & valuation: Time value of money
text: A dollar today is worth more than a dollar next year, because today's dollar can be invested and because the future is uncertain. To compare money at different times, discount future amounts back to today: Present value = Future amount ÷ (1 + rate)^years Made-up example: $1,000 received in 3 years at a 10% rate = 1,000 ÷ 1.1^3 ≈ $751.31 today

title: Lesson 3: Funding & valuation: How businesses are valued
text: Multiples: value = a profit or revenue figure × a multiple seen in similar businesses. Small private businesses often sell for roughly 2–5× their yearly owner earnings; it varies widely. Discounted cash flow (DCF): forecast future cash flows and discount each one to today. It's correct in theory but very sensitive to assumptions. Small changes to the growth or discount rate swing the answer enormously. Assets: what the things it owns would sell for. Mainly used as a floor, or for asset-heavy businesses. Honest caveat: valuation is part maths, part negotiation. A business is worth what a buyer will actually pay, and that links straight to the next lesson. ← 2. Investing4. How a business makes money →

title: Lesson 6: Why businesses exist, and what's changing now
text: > The 30-second version Businesses exist because people pay to have problems solved. Profit is the reward for solving a problem better or cheaper than the alternatives. Today, one person with cheap online tools can start what once needed a team.

title: Lesson 6: Why businesses exist, and what's changing now: The main reason a business exists
text: A problem people have + a solution they'll pay for + a way to deliver it for less than they pay = a business If any part is missing, it's a hobby or a charity, not a business. No real problem: nobody buys. Nobody will pay: no income. Costs more to deliver than they pay: every sale loses money.

title: Lesson 6: Why businesses exist, and what's changing now: Who a business serves
text: Customers get a problem solved. Owners and investors get a return for the risk and money they put in. Workers and suppliers get paid. The community gets jobs, products and taxes. The businesses that last keep all four reasonably happy. Squeezing one group hard usually comes back to bite.

title: Lesson 6: Why businesses exist, and what's changing now: What's changing now
text: Change What it means for you AI tools Writing, design, research and coding help are cheap or free, so one person can do the work of a small team. Your competitors have the same tools, so your edge is knowing your customer. Audience first Many new businesses start by building an audience online, then selling to it. Trust comes before the sale. Solo and small businesses Online stores, payment links and website builders mean you can start with very little money. Subscriptions Steady monthly income is attractive, but people now cancel subscriptions they don't use. You must keep earning it. Reviews and trust Buyers check reviews before they buy. Honest, real proof matters more than ever. Straight talk Trends change quickly, and some of these will look different in a year. The rule underneath doesn't change: solve a real problem, for people who'll pay, for less than they pay. New tools make that faster, not optional. Try it Write your idea in the formula above: the problem, the solution, who pays, and what it costs you to deliver. If you can't fill one line in, that's the part to work on first. ← 5. Financial statements7. Buy back your time →

title: Lesson 7: Buy back your time
text: > The 30-second version Work out your "buyback rate": what an hour of your time is really worth. Hand off tasks that cost less than that rate and drain your energy. Teach once by recording yourself, so you don't have to explain twice.

title: Lesson 7: Buy back your time: 1. Your buyback rate
text: Your hourly value = yearly income ÷ 2,000 working hours Buyback rate = your hourly value ÷ 4 Example: $60,000 a year ÷ 2,000 = $30 an hour $30 ÷ 4 = $7.50 an hour Any task you could pay someone less than your buyback rate to do is a task to hand off when you can afford it. Dividing by 4 keeps it safe: you only buy back time when it's clearly cheap compared with what your time earns.

title: Lesson 7: Buy back your time: 2. Sort your tasks: the DRIP idea
text: Type of task Makes money? Gives you energy? What to do Delegate Little No, drains you Hand it off first (admin, scheduling, inbox) Replace Yes No, drains you Train or hire someone to take it over Invest Not yet Yes Keep time for it: learning, health, relationships Produce Yes Yes This is your best work. Spend more time here.

title: Lesson 7: Buy back your time: 3. Teach once: record yourself
text: Martell calls it the camcorder method. Next time you do a task you want to hand off, record your screen or film yourself doing it and talk through each step. That video becomes the training, so you never explain it twice.

title: Lesson 7: Buy back your time: 4. Bring solutions, not just problems: the 1-3-1 rule
text: 1 problem, stated clearly 3 possible solutions 1 recommendation: the one you'd pick, and why Use it when a team member brings you a problem, and use it yourself when you go to a mentor or investor. It turns "What should I do?" into a decision. Straight talk When you're just starting with little money, you may not be able to pay anyone yet. Start with free time-savers: templates, recorded how-tos, AI tools, and saying no to low-value work. These are our simple explanations of Martell's ideas; read his book for the full version. Sharp isn't connected to or endorsed by him. Try it Write down everything you did yesterday. Mark each task D, R, I or P. Pick one D task and find a way to hand it off, automate it or drop it this week. ← 6. Why businesses exist8. Using AI at work →

title: Lesson 8: Using AI at work without the headaches
text: > The 30-second version Count checking time: AI is only worth it if writing plus checking beats doing it yourself. Never let AI tell customers prices, rules or promises without a person checking. Keep your best prompts saved, test them monthly, and never paste private info into free tools.

title: Lesson 8: Using AI at work without the headaches: 1. Count the checking, not just the writing
text: AI writes in seconds, but someone has to check it. If checking takes 20 minutes, that's the real cost. Track a task for a week: time without AI vs time with AI including checking. The AI savings calculator does the maths.

title: Lesson 8: Using AI at work without the headaches: 2. AI makes confident mistakes
text: AI can invent a price, a refund rule or a fact, and say it like it's certain. Rules that keep you safe: Anything with a number, a promise or a policy gets checked by a person before a customer sees it. Give the AI your real price list and rules to copy from, and tell it to say "I'll check with the team" when it isn't sure. Start AI on inside jobs (drafts, summaries, ideas) before customer-facing ones.

title: Lesson 8: Using AI at work without the headaches: 3. "It worked yesterday": test your prompts
text: AI companies update their tools, and a prompt that worked last month can start giving different answers. Keep your best prompts in one shared place, like the prompt library, not in one person's chat history, and re-test each one every month.

title: Lesson 8: Using AI at work without the headaches: 4. Don't paste private info
text: Customer emails, phone numbers, card numbers, contracts and passwords don't belong in free AI tools. Check what the tool's settings say about saving and training on your data, use a business plan where possible, and run text through the before-you-paste check first.

title: Lesson 8: Using AI at work without the headaches: 5. If you build AI for clients: demo vs daily
text: What clients saw What to tell them up front A perfect demo on social media "A demo works once. We'll test it on 50 of your real examples before you rely on it." "It can do anything" "This version does three things well. Anything else is a new quote." "It never makes mistakes" "It will sometimes be wrong. Here's how a person checks the important parts."

title: Lesson 8: Using AI at work without the headaches: 6. Fewer tools, connected
text: A new AI tool launches every week. Pick one or two, learn them well, and cancel the rest; the AI cost check shows what unused ones waste. Then cut the copy-paste work: many apps can pass AI results straight into your spreadsheet, email or customer list with built-in integrations or automation tools that connect apps. The next lesson shows how to set that up safely. Straight talk AI changes fast, so tools and prices here will change too. The habits don't: check what matters, protect private info, measure the real time saved, and keep a person responsible for what customers see. Try it Pick one task you use AI for. Time it for a week with checking included, save the prompt in the prompt library, and write one rule for what must be checked by a person. ← 7. Buy back your time9. Automate with AI →

title: Lesson 9: Automate your business with AI
text: > The 30-second version Every automation is "when this happens, do that". AI can do the writing or sorting step in the middle. Only automate jobs that repeat, follow the same rules, and are cheap to get wrong. Start with AI writing drafts you approve. Let it run on its own only after it has been right again and again.

title: Lesson 9: Automate your business with AI: 1. How an automation works
text: Every automation has three parts: Trigger → Steps → Result Trigger: a customer fills in my order form Steps: add it to my sheet, AI drafts a thank-you Result: I check it and tap send Before AI, the steps could only copy and move things. Now an AI step can also write (a reply, a caption, a description), sort (is this message an order, a question or a complaint?) and sum up (this week's messages in five lines).

title: Lesson 9: Automate your business with AI: 2. What to automate: the 3R test
text: A job is worth automating only if it passes all three: Repeats: you do it at least every week. A one-time job isn't worth the setup. Rules: you do it the same way every time. If each one needs fresh judgment, keep it. Risk is low: a mistake is cheap and easy to fix. Anything with money, promises or upset customers stays with a person. Job 3R test Verdict "Got your order" message with details from the order form Repeats, same every time, details copied not invented Automate Answering the 5 questions customers always ask Repeats, same answers, low risk if the answers come from your own list AI drafts, you approve Writing a week of social captions from one idea Repeats, simple rules, nothing goes out until you post it AI drafts, you approve Replying to an angry customer Different every time, high risk You, always Deciding your prices Rare, needs judgment, big risk You, always

title: Lesson 9: Automate your business with AI: 3. Five automations you can set up this week
text: Order form to spreadsheet. Many free form tools can drop every answer straight into a spreadsheet. No more copying orders by hand. Saved answers for common questions. Write your 5 best answers once (or have AI tidy them up), save them as quick replies in your messaging app, and reuse them. A week of posts in 20 minutes. Give AI one product and your customer, ask for 7 caption ideas, edit them, then use your social app's built-in scheduler. Payment reminders. Use your payment app's reminder feature, or a calendar reminder with a saved polite message, so nobody forgets to pay you. Monday summary. Your spreadsheet adds up last week's sales with formulas. AI can turn the totals into a short "what went well, what to fix" note. The maths stays in the spreadsheet, never in the AI. Apps that connect other apps (called no-code automation tools) can chain these together, like form → sheet → email draft. Learn one app well before adding more.

title: Lesson 9: Automate your business with AI: 4. Keep a person in the loop
text: Move up these levels slowly. Most small businesses should live at level 2 for a long time. Level What happens Use it for 1. Helper You ask AI, you copy what's useful Ideas, first drafts 2. Draft and approve The automation writes; nothing goes out until you tap send Customer replies, posts, emails 3. On its own It sends by itself; you check a few each week Only jobs that passed the 3R test and were right many times in a row AI can invent a delivery date, a discount or a refund rule and sound sure about it. Anything with a number, date, price or promise gets a person's check before a customer sees it.

title: Lesson 9: Automate your business with AI: 5. Do the maths first
text: Weeks to pay back = setup hours ÷ hours saved per week Monthly value = (hours saved − hours checking) × your hourly value − tool cost Example: setting up saved replies takes 3 hours and saves 1 hour a week, so it pays back in 3 weeks. A $10-a-month tool that saves 3 hours but needs 1 hour of checking, with your time worth $12 an hour, is worth (3 − 1) × 12 − 10 = $14 a month. The AI savings calculator does this for you.

title: Lesson 9: Automate your business with AI: 6. Stay safe
text: Check the age rules. Many AI and automation apps require you to be 13, and some 18. Read the sign-up rules and get a parent's OK. Never automate money moving out, passwords or anything you couldn't undo. Keep private info out. Customer emails, addresses and card numbers don't go into free AI tools. Use first names and order details only. Keep an off switch. Know how to pause each automation in one tap, and check it the first few times it runs. Straight talk Automating a messy process just makes the mess faster. Do the job by hand a few times until the steps are clear, then automate. And customers can tell when nobody is home: keep the personal touches, like a real thank-you or a quick voice note, done by you. Try it List every task you did for your business last week. Run each through the 3R test. Pick the one that passes and saves the most time, work out its payback with the formula, and set it up at level 2: drafts you approve. ← 8. Using AI at work10. Marketing basics →

title: Lesson 10: Marketing basics
text: > The 30-second version Pick one specific customer, not everyone. Say why you in one sentence. Lead with the benefit; use the feature as proof.

title: Lesson 10: Marketing basics: Pick one customer, not everyone
text: "My product is for everyone" means your message lands with no one. Describe one specific customer so clearly you could find ten of them this week: Who they are: "first-time landlords with one or two rental units", not "property owners". What problem they have that they'd pay to fix. Where they already spend time: groups, sites, events, newsletters. What they use now instead of you. That's your real competition, even if it's a spreadsheet or "doing nothing". A narrow start isn't a ceiling. Win one group, then expand to the next.

title: Lesson 10: Marketing basics: Positioning: say why you, in one sentence
text: For [customer] who [problem], [product] is the [category] that [main benefit]. Unlike [alternative], we [key difference]. Example: "For first-time landlords who dread tax season, RentLedger is the bookkeeping app that sorts every receipt automatically. Unlike a spreadsheet, it's ready for your accountant in one click." That sentence is your positioning. Test it on a stranger. If they can't repeat what you do and who it's for after 5 seconds, simplify.

title: Lesson 10: Marketing basics: Benefits beat features
text: Feature (what it is) Benefit (what it does for them) Automatic receipt scanning No more shoebox of receipts in April Meals delivered on Sunday Five evenings a week back with your kids 24/7 support Your site never stays down overnight Lead with the benefit; use the feature as proof.

title: Lesson 10: Marketing basics: The offer is part of the marketing
text: What exactly do they get, for how much, and what happens if it doesn't work? A clear price, a simple bundle and a fair guarantee often lift sales more than a better ad. Straight talk The most common first-time mistake is buying ads before knowing who the customer is. Ads amplify a message. If the message is vague, they amplify nothing, at your expense. ← 9. Automate with AI11. Getting customers →

title: Lesson 11: Getting customers
text: > The 30-second version Your first customers come from people you can reach directly. Pick one or two channels and do them well. Own your audience with email. Ads come last.

title: Lesson 11: Getting customers: The main channels
text: Channel Cost Speed Best for Direct outreach (messages, calls, your network) Time Fast Your first 10 customers Communities (groups, forums, local events) Time Fast Niche audiences; help first, pitch second Referrals and word of mouth Low Medium Once people love the product Short video and social posts Time Medium Showing, not telling; builds trust Content and search (articles, tools) Time Slow (months) Long-term free traffic that compounds Email list Low Medium Turning interest into sales; you own it Paid ads Money Fast Scaling something that already sells Partnerships Shared Medium Borrowing someone else's audience

title: Lesson 11: Getting customers: The funnel
text: Every sale moves through the same stages. Most businesses lose people at one stage in particular. Find yours and fix that first. Aware → they hear about you Interested → they visit, follow or sign up Decide → they compare, ask questions, read reviews Buy → they pay Return → they buy again and tell friends

title: Lesson 11: Getting customers: Rules that save money
text: Your first customers come from people you can reach directly. Don't wait for strangers to find you. Focus on one or two channels. Five half-done channels usually lose to one done properly. Own your audience. Social followers can disappear if a platform changes its rules. An email list is yours. Ads come last. Spend on ads once you know your message and your numbers. Then they pour fuel on something that already works. Try it List 20 people who match your customer and could hear from you this week. Message 10 of them. Ask about the problem, not your product. Their words become your marketing copy. ← 10. Marketing basics12. Measuring marketing →

title: Lesson 12: Measuring marketing
text: > The 30-second version Five numbers matter: conversion rate, CAC, ROAS, LTV and payback. Likes and views feel good; sales pay the bills. Change one thing at a time so you know what worked.

title: Lesson 12: Measuring marketing: The five numbers
text: Conversion rate = people who did it ÷ people who could have CAC (cost per customer) = marketing spend ÷ new customers ROAS (return on ad spend) = revenue from ads ÷ ad spend LTV (lifetime value) = revenue per month × gross margin × months they stay Payback = CAC ÷ (revenue per month × gross margin) Worked example: you spend $600 and win 12 customers. CAC = $50. Each pays $25 a month at a 60% margin and stays 10 months: LTV = 25 × 0.6 × 10 = $150. LTV:CAC = 3:1, the common healthy guideline. Payback = 50 ÷ 15 = 3.3 months.

title: Lesson 12: Measuring marketing: Vanity numbers vs real numbers
text: Feels good Actually matters Followers, likes, views Sign-ups and sales from those views Website visits Conversion rate of those visits Email list size Revenue per subscriber Ad clicks Profit after the ad bill

title: Lesson 12: Measuring marketing: Test one thing at a time
text: Change one element (headline, price, image) and keep everything else the same. Wait for enough results. A handful of visitors can swing by luck; small tests mislead. Track where people come from with tagged links (UTM tags) and a simple analytics tool, so you know which channel earned the sale. Straight talk Benchmarks you read online ("a good conversion rate is 3%") vary wildly by industry and traffic source. Your own numbers, measured consistently, beat any average. Run your own numbers in the marketing calculators. ← 11. Getting customers13. Words that sell →

title: Lesson 13: Words that sell
text: > The 30-second version Say what they get, in words they already use. Every message needs four parts: the problem, your promise, proof, and one clear ask. Cut every word that doesn't help someone say yes.

title: Lesson 13: Words that sell: The four parts of any message that sells
text: Problem: name the pain in their words "Tax season stresses you out?" Promise: what changes for them "Get every receipt sorted in one click." Proof: why they should believe you "Used by 40 local landlords." Ask: one clear next step "Start your free trial." It works for a website, a social post, a cold email or a flyer. If one part is missing, people stall. No problem: they don't care. No proof: they don't believe. No ask: they don't act.

title: Lesson 13: Words that sell: Headlines: specific beats clever
text: Weak Strong Why "Welcome to Fresh Bites" "Healthy dinners at your door by 6pm" Says what they get "Innovative tutoring solutions" "Raise your maths grade in 6 weeks" A result and a time "Best bakery in town!" "Gluten-free birthday cakes, ordered by Thursday" Specific, believable A good headline passes the five-second test: a stranger knows what you do and who it's for.

title: Lesson 13: Words that sell: Use their words, not yours
text: The best copy is stolen from your customers. When you talk to them (see Getting customers), write down their exact phrases. If they say "I'm drowning in receipts", that line will sell better than anything you'd write yourself.

title: Lesson 13: Words that sell: The ask: one action, verb first
text: One ask per message. "Follow, share, buy and sign up" means they do nothing. Start with a verb and say what happens: "Get my free plan" beats "Submit". Lower the risk: "Free for 3 days, no card needed" makes saying yes easier. Straight talk Never invent reviews, numbers or fake deadlines. It destroys trust when people find out, and in the US fake reviews and testimonials can break consumer-protection law. Real proof, even small ("my first 5 customers came back"), is enough. Try it Write your offer in the four parts: problem, promise, proof, ask. Read it to someone for five seconds, then ask them what you sell. If they can't say it back, cut words until they can. ← 12. Measuring marketing14. Social media and short video →

title: Lesson 14: Social media and short video
text: > The 30-second version Pick one platform where your customers already spend time. Hook people in the first two seconds, then teach or show one useful thing. Followers can vanish if a platform changes. Move them to your email list.

title: Lesson 14: Social media and short video: Pick one platform first
text: Platform Good for TikTok, Instagram Reels, YouTube Shorts Being discovered by strangers with short videos YouTube (longer videos) Answering questions people search for; videos keep getting found for years LinkedIn Selling to businesses and professionals Facebook groups, local communities Local businesses and tight-knit niches Where do your customers already scroll? Start there. One platform done well beats four done badly.

title: Lesson 14: Social media and short video: The shape of a good post
text: Hook: first 2 seconds, why should they stop? "3 money mistakes I made at 19" Value: one useful idea, shown not told show the mistake and the fix Proof: a result, a screen, a before and after your real numbers Ask: one next step "Free budget tool, link in bio"

title: Lesson 14: Social media and short video: Never run out of ideas
text: Answer a question a customer actually asked you. Before and after: the problem, then the result. Behind the scenes: how you make it, what went wrong. Myth vs fact in your area. A mistake you made and what you learned. People trust honesty.

title: Lesson 14: Social media and short video: What to measure
text: Likes are a vanity number (see Measuring marketing). Watch what moves people towards buying: saves, shares, comments, clicks to your site and email sign-ups. A common rule of thumb is to post on a steady schedule, such as three times a week, for a few months before judging whether a platform works. Straight talk Going viral is mostly luck, and a viral post from the wrong audience sells nothing. A small group of the right people, who see you every week, is what builds a business. Never buy followers: it ruins your reach and fools no one. Try it Write five hooks for your business, each under ten words. Film the best one as a 30-second video this week. Count the saves, shares and link clicks, not the likes. ← 13. Words that sell15. Negotiation →

title: Lesson 15: Negotiation
text: > The 30-second version Your power is your alternative if the deal fails. Decide your walk-away point before you start. Trade concessions. Never give them away for free.

title: Lesson 15: Negotiation: Step 1: prepare four numbers and one plan
text: BATNA (Best Alternative To a Negotiated Agreement): what you'll actually do if this deal fails. Another job offer? Another supplier? Staying put? Your BATNA is your power. Improve it before you negotiate. Walk-away point (reservation price): the worst deal you'll accept. Set it from your BATNA, and set it before you're in the room. Target: an ambitious but defensible outcome. People who aim higher tend to get more. Their side: estimate their BATNA and walk-away point too. The ZOPA (Zone Of Possible Agreement) is the overlap between your walk-away point and theirs. If a seller won't go below $8,000 and a buyer won't go above $10,000, the ZOPA is $8,000–$10,000. If there's no overlap, no deal is possible on price alone, so you'll need to change the deal itself. Any price inside the green zone works for both sides. Where in the zone the deal lands depends on anchoring, information and who can walk away.

title: Lesson 15: Negotiation: Step 2: interests, not positions
text: A position is what someone says they want ("I need $90k"). An interest is why ("I need to cover my rent and feel valued"). Two sisters fight over one orange and split it in half. One wanted the juice, the other the peel for baking; they could have had 100% each. Ask why to find trades that cost you little and are worth a lot to them.

title: Lesson 15: Negotiation: Step 3: anchor deliberately
text: The first number on the table pulls the final result towards it. That's anchoring. If you know the market well, consider making the first offer, ambitious but with a reason attached. If you don't know the market, let them go first, or anchor with research ("Similar roles pay $85–95k"). If they anchor extreme, don't counter off their number. Name it ("That's far from what we're seeing") and re-anchor with your own reasoning.

title: Lesson 15: Negotiation: Step 4: listen more than you talk
text: Ask open questions: "What would make this work for you?" "How did you arrive at that number?" Calibrated "how" questions push the problem back to them: "How am I supposed to do that on this budget?" Label emotions: "It sounds like timing is the real pressure here." Use silence. After you make an offer or hear one, stop talking. People fill silence with concessions and information.

title: Lesson 15: Negotiation: Step 5: trade, don't give
text: Never make a concession for free. Use "If you can do X, I can do Y." Make each concession smaller than the last. It signals you're near your limit. Negotiate several things at once (price, timing, scope, payment terms, extras). Single-issue haggling is win/lose; multi-issue deals let both sides win. Don't split the difference early. It rewards whoever anchored more extremely.

title: Lesson 15: Negotiation: Common mistakes
text: Negotiating against yourself: lowering your ask before they've responded. Revealing your walk-away point. Accepting the first offer: it signals you left money on the table, and often leaves both sides less happy. Treating it as a fight: you may work with this person for years. Be hard on the problem, soft on the person. Not preparing a BATNA: walking in with no alternative is the single biggest weakness. Ethics and self-interest agree here Don't lie about facts ("I have another offer" when you don't). It's often illegal in contracts, it's easy to call out, and it ruins trust. You're allowed to decline to share information ("I'd rather not get into my current salary"). ← 14. Social media and short video16. Negotiation scripts →

title: Lesson 16: Negotiation scripts
text: > The 30-second version Make your ask, then stop talking. Bring results and market data, not personal needs. Cut scope, not price.

title: Lesson 16: Negotiation scripts: Salary — new job offer
text: When they ask your expectations early: "I'd like to learn more about the role before naming a number. What's the budgeted range?" When the offer arrives: "Thank you. I'm excited about this role and the team. Based on [market data / my experience with X], I was expecting something closer to [target]. Is there flexibility on base?" Then stop talking. If base is fixed: "I understand. Could we look at a signing bonus, extra leave, a title change, or a salary review at six months?"

title: Lesson 16: Negotiation scripts: Raise at your current job
text: "I'd like to talk about my compensation. Over the last year I [concrete result with a number: grew X by 20%, saved $Y, took on Z]. Market data for this role shows [range]. I'm asking for an adjustment to [number]. What would it take to get there?" Bring results, not needs. "My rent went up" is your problem; "I saved the company $40k" is theirs.

title: Lesson 16: Negotiation scripts: Buying something (car, equipment, services)
text: "I'm ready to buy this week, and I'm comparing it with [alternative]. What's the best out-the-door price you can do?" Then: "That's above what I can do. If you can get to [number], we can sign today." Negotiate the total price, not the monthly payment. Monthly payments hide a longer loan and extras.

title: Lesson 16: Negotiation scripts: Selling / pricing your services
text: When a client says it's too expensive: "I understand. Which part of the project matters most to you? We could reduce the scope to fit your budget rather than reduce the quality." Cut scope, not price. Discounting trains clients to push back every time.

title: Lesson 16: Negotiation scripts: Rent or a bill
text: "I've been a reliable tenant/customer for [time] and I'd like to stay. Similar places nearby are listed at [number]. If I sign a [longer] lease, could we keep the rent at [number]?"

title: Lesson 16: Negotiation scripts: Preparation sheet (fill this before any negotiation)
text: Question Your answer What do I actually want, and why (my interests)? What's my BATNA if this fails? Walk-away point Target (ambitious + reason) What do they want, and why? Their likely BATNA Things cheap for me but valuable to them Questions I'll ask ← 15. Negotiation17. Getting people to say yes →

title: Lesson 17: Getting people to say yes
text: > The 30-second version Listen first, then show what's in it for them. Make the ask small and clear. Treat objections as questions: acknowledge, ask, answer, check.

title: Lesson 17: Getting people to say yes: 1. Listen before you pitch
text: Ask what they want and what worries them, then repeat it back in your own words: "So the real concern is the timeline, not the price?" People say yes far more readily to someone who has shown they understand the problem.

title: Lesson 17: Getting people to say yes: 2. Make it about them
text: Your reasons are not their reasons. Translate every point into what they get. About you About them "I need this deal to hit my target." "This gets your launch done two weeks early." "Our product has 40 features." "You'll stop doing the invoicing by hand."

title: Lesson 17: Getting people to say yes: 3. Make the ask small and clear
text: A vague ask gets a vague answer. Say exactly what you want, and make the first step easy: "Can we try it for one month?" is easier to agree to than "Will you sign a year-long contract?"

title: Lesson 17: Getting people to say yes: 4. Back it up honestly
text: Proof: a number, a result, a short example. "Three local gyms use it" beats "it's great". Give first: share something useful before you ask. People like to return a favour. Be consistent: link your ask to something they've already said they want.

title: Lesson 17: Getting people to say yes: 5. Treat objections as questions
text: An objection usually means "I'm not sure yet", not "no". Answer the worry behind it: Acknowledge: "That's fair, price matters." Ask: "Compared with what you're using now?" Answer: one clear reason, with proof. Check: "Does that cover it?" Straight talk Fake scarcity ("only 2 left!"), invented deadlines and pressure tactics can win one yes and lose the relationship. If the deal is good for them, honest persuasion is enough. If it isn't, it shouldn't happen. ← 16. Negotiation scripts18. Pitching investors, simply →

title: Lesson 18: Pitching investors, simply
text: > The 30-second version Problem, solution, proof, market, why you, the ask: in 60 seconds. Know your numbers: revenue, growth, margin, CAC and LTV, burn and runway. Runway = cash ÷ monthly burn.

title: Lesson 18: Pitching investors, simply: The pitch in six lines
text: 1. Problem: who has it, and how much it hurts 2. Solution: what you do about it, in one sentence 3. Proof: customers, sales, growth (traction) 4. Market: how many people have this problem 5. Why you: why your team wins 6. The ask: how much you're raising and what it pays for Practise saying the whole thing in 60 seconds. If you can't, it isn't clear yet.

title: Lesson 18: Pitching investors, simply: The numbers they'll ask about
text: Number Plain English Revenue and growth How much you sell, and how fast that's rising each month Gross margin How much of each sale you keep after direct costs CAC and LTV What a customer costs to win vs what they're worth Burn rate How much cash you spend each month beyond what comes in Runway Months until the cash runs out: cash ÷ burn rate Use of funds Exactly what the money will pay for, and what it will achieve Runway = cash in the bank ÷ monthly burn Example: $90,000 ÷ $15,000 a month = 6 months

title: Lesson 18: Pitching investors, simply: What makes investors nervous
text: Not knowing your own numbers. "We have no competition." Everyone has competition, even if it's doing nothing. Huge market claims with no customers yet. Not being able to say what the money is for. Remember Investors are buying a share of your company, so this is a negotiation too. Your BATNA (another investor, or growing without them) is your power. The Funding & valuation lesson explains dilution. ← 17. Getting people to say yes19. Staying calm under pressure →

title: Lesson 19: Staying calm under pressure
text: > The 30-second version Prepare the 20 hardest questions before the meeting. Pause, give the answer in one sentence, then explain. "I don't know, here's how I'll find out" beats a confident guess.

title: Lesson 19: Staying calm under pressure: Before: prepare the hard questions
text: Write down the 20 questions you'd least like to be asked, and an answer for each. Most tough questions are predictable: your numbers (especially your runway and burn rate), your competition, your biggest risk, why you, and why now. Practise them out loud with a timer, using the Investor pressure drill.

title: Lesson 19: Staying calm under pressure: During: five habits
text: Pause. Two seconds of silence before answering looks thoughtful, not lost. Answer first, then explain. Lead with the answer in one sentence, then give one or two reasons. Rambling is what pressure looks like. Clarify if you need to. "Do you mean this year's numbers or the forecast?" buys time and avoids answering the wrong question. Say "I don't know" well. "I don't know that number exactly. It's around X, and I'll send the exact figure tomorrow." Then actually send it. Guessing confidently and being wrong is far worse. Steer back to your strengths. Answer the question honestly, then connect it to something you're confident about: "That's a real risk, and here's how we're testing it."

title: Lesson 19: Staying calm under pressure: In your body
text: Box breathing (before you walk in, or during a pause): breathe in 4 seconds → hold 4 → breathe out 4 → hold 4 Repeat 3 times. Slow your speaking pace a little more than feels natural. Nerves speed you up; slower sounds sure.

title: Lesson 19: Staying calm under pressure: Hostile or unfair questions
text: Stay polite and specific. Acknowledge the concern, answer with facts, and don't argue tone. "Fair challenge. Here's what our data shows…" You're also judging whether you want this investor. How they treat you now is how they'll treat you when things go wrong. Straight talk No technique replaces knowing your numbers. Most pressure in investor meetings comes from not being sure of your own business. Learn the numbers cold, and most of the nerves go with it. ← 18. Pitching investors, simply20. Your voice in the room →

title: Lesson 20: Your voice in the room
text: > The 30-second version Speak slower than feels natural, and pause on purpose. End sentences with your voice going down, not up, so they sound sure. Record yourself, watch it back, fix one thing at a time.

title: Lesson 20: Your voice in the room: Five voice habits
text: Slow down. Nerves speed you up. Slower sounds confident and gives you time to think. Pause instead of "um". A one-second silence sounds thoughtful. Fillers like "um", "like" and "basically" sound unsure. Land your sentences. Let your voice drop at the end of a statement. Rising at the end makes facts sound like questions. Breathe from your belly. Short chest breaths make your voice thin and shaky. Breathe in slowly before you start. Stress the number. "We grew 40% last quarter." Leaning on the key word tells them what matters.

title: Lesson 20: Your voice in the room: Your body speaks too
text: Do Avoid Sit or stand tall, feet flat Slouching or rocking Look at the person who asked, then the others Staring at your slides or notes Calm hands that show size or steps Fidgeting with a pen or phone A real smile when you meet them A frozen, nervous face On a video call: put the camera at eye level, look at the lens when you make your key point, and sit facing a window or lamp so they can see your face.

title: Lesson 20: Your voice in the room: How to practise (15 minutes a day)
text: 1. Record your 60-second pitch on your phone. 2. Watch it once with the sound off: check your body. 3. Watch it with the sound on: count your "um"s. 4. Fix ONE thing, record again. 5. Then pitch it to a friend and ask: "What do you remember?" Straight talk Nobody expects a perfect speaker. Investors expect you to know your business and tell the truth. A slightly nervous founder who knows their numbers beats a smooth talker who doesn't. Try it Record your one-sentence pitch three times today: once fast, once slow, once slow with a pause before your best number. Listen back. The third one almost always sounds the most convincing. ← 19. Staying calm under pressure21. Getting an investor interested →

title: Lesson 21: Getting an investor interested
text: > The 30-second version Lead with your strongest proof: real customers, sales or growth. A warm introduction from someone they trust beats a cold email. Pick investors who back businesses like yours, and follow up with progress.

title: Lesson 21: Getting an investor interested: What makes an investor lean in
text: Signal Example Traction (proof people want it) "140 paying customers in 4 months, most found us by word of mouth." A big, painful problem "Small landlords lose a weekend every tax season." Why you "I ran rentals for 5 years and built this to fix my own problem." Why now "New rules this year force every landlord to keep digital records."

title: Lesson 21: Getting an investor interested: Your one-line hook
text: We help [who] [get what result], and we've already [your best proof]. Example: "We help first-time landlords finish their taxes in an hour, and 140 already pay us every month." Use it as your email's first line and your first sentence in the room.

title: Lesson 21: Getting an investor interested: Getting the meeting
text: Make a target list. Look for investors who have backed businesses at your stage and in your area. Don't pitch someone who never invests in your kind of business. Find a warm introduction. Ask a founder, mentor or teacher who knows them. A short note they can forward helps. Keep the first email short: your hook, three proof points, and one ask: a 20-minute call. Follow up with progress, not "just checking in". "Since we wrote, we added 30 customers" is a reason to reply.

title: Lesson 21: Getting an investor interested: In the meeting: make them want more
text: Open with the hook, then let them ask questions. Questions mean interest. Ask them: "What would you need to see to invest?" Their answer is your to-do list. End with a clear next step and date, and send a short thank-you note the same day. Straight talk Never fake interest from other investors or invent deadlines to create pressure. Investors talk to each other, and one lie can close every door. Real progress is the only pressure that works. Try it Write your one-line hook, then list five people who could introduce you to an investor or a mentor. Contact one this week. ← 20. Your voice in the room22. Getting the best out of investors →

title: Lesson 22: Getting the best out of investors
text: > The 30-second version You're choosing them too: check their reputation with founders they've backed. Ask for specific help: introductions, hiring, advice. Send short monthly updates, good news and bad.

title: Lesson 22: Getting the best out of investors: Before you say yes: check them out
text: Talk to two founders they've backed, including one whose business struggled. How did the investor act when things went wrong? Ask what help they give besides money, and for an example. Read the terms with a lawyer. Money with bad terms can cost you more than no money (see Funding & valuation).

title: Lesson 22: Getting the best out of investors: Questions to ask an investor
text: "How do you help after you invest? Give me a real example." "What happens if we miss our plan?" "How involved do you like to be?" "Who else could you introduce us to?"

title: Lesson 22: Getting the best out of investors: After they invest: use them well
text: Ask for Example Introductions "Could you introduce us to two people who buy for small landlords?" Hiring help "Do you know a part-time bookkeeper we could hire?" Advice on one decision "Should we raise prices now or after launch? Here are our numbers." Specific asks get specific help. "Let me know if you can help" gets nothing.

title: Lesson 22: Getting the best out of investors: The monthly update
text: Wins: 1 to 3, with numbers Numbers: sales, customers, cash, months of runway Problems: one honest one Asks: one specific thing they can help with Send it every month, even in bad months. Investors who hear bad news early help. Investors who are surprised stop trusting you. Straight talk An investor's advice is input, not orders, unless your agreement says otherwise. Listen, thank them, then decide. It's your business, and you'll live with the result. Try it Write next month's update in the four lines above, even if you don't have investors yet. It's the fastest way to see what's working, and it becomes your first investor email. ← 21. Getting an investor interestedCalculators →

title: Glossary
text: > Anchoring The first number put on the table, which pulls the final deal towards it. APR Annual percentage rate — the yearly cost of borrowing, including some fees. Asset Something you own that has value: cash, equipment, property, money owed to you. BATNA Best Alternative To a Negotiated Agreement — what you'll do if no deal happens. Bond A loan you make to a government or company in exchange for interest. Break-even The sales level where revenue exactly covers all costs: zero profit, zero loss. Burn rate How much more cash a business spends each month than it brings in. Buyback rate What an hour of your time is worth ÷ 4. Tasks you can pay someone less than this to do are worth handing off (an idea from Dan Martell). CAC Customer acquisition cost — sales and marketing spend ÷ new customers won. Call to action The one next step you ask people to take, like "Start your free trial". Cash flow Money actually moving in and out of the bank, as opposed to accounting profit. Channel A way customers find you: social media, search, ads, word of mouth, partnerships. Churn The share of customers who stop buying or cancel in a period. COGS Cost of goods sold — direct costs of making or buying what you sold. Compound interest Earning interest on previous interest, so growth accelerates over time. Concession Something you give up in a negotiation, ideally in exchange for something back. Contribution margin

title: Glossary
text: Price minus variable cost per unit — what each sale adds towards fixed costs. Conversion rate The share of people who take an action, such as buying, out of everyone who could have. Copywriting Writing words that persuade people to act: headlines, posts, emails, pages. Dilution Your ownership percentage shrinking when new shares are issued to investors. Diversification Spreading money across many investments so one failure doesn't sink you. Equity Ownership. On a balance sheet: assets minus liabilities. Expense ratio The yearly fee a fund charges, as a percentage of your money in it. Filler words Sounds like "um", "uh" and "like" that fill silence and make you sound unsure. Funnel The stages people move through on the way to buying: aware, interested, decide, buy. Gross margin (Revenue − cost of goods) ÷ revenue: how much of each sale you keep after direct costs. Hook The first line or first two seconds of a post, made to stop people scrolling. Index fund A fund that buys everything in a market index instead of picking stocks. Usually very cheap. Inflation The general rise in prices over time, which reduces what money can buy. Liability Something you owe: loans, unpaid bills, taxes due. Liquidity How quickly something can be turned into cash without losing value. LTV Lifetime value — gross profit you expect from a customer over the whole relationship. Markup Profit ÷ cost. Not the same as margin. Net profit

title: Glossary
text: What's left after every cost, interest payment and tax. Objection A reason someone gives for not saying yes yet, often a question in disguise. Pitch A short, clear explanation of your business and what you're asking for. Positioning One clear sentence on who you're for, what you do for them, and why you instead of the alternative. Present value What a future amount of money is worth today, after discounting. Receivables Money customers owe you for things already delivered. Reservation price Your walk-away point in a negotiation. ROAS Return on ad spend: revenue from ads divided by what the ads cost. Runway How many months until the cash runs out: cash in the bank ÷ monthly burn rate. Traction Proof that people want your product: customers, sales, growth. Use of funds What an investor's money will pay for, and what it will achieve. Valuation An estimate of what a business is worth. Warm introduction Being introduced to someone by a person they already know and trust. ZOPA Zone Of Possible Agreement — the overlap between both sides' walk-away points.
